ai.definition: Co-Packaged Optics is a technology that integrates optical components directly onto the same package as the silicon-based electronics (such as ASICs) to facilitate faster and more efficient data transmission between chips.
ai.howItWorks: By placing photonic components adjacent to the electronic components, co-packaged optics reduces the distance over which electrical signals must be converted to light and back again. This minimizes signal loss and enables higher bandwidth with lower power consumption compared to traditional optical interconnects that are separate from the electronics.
ai.problemSolved: High-speed data communication between silicon-based devices is constrained by electrical interconnect limitations, leading to increased latency and energy consumption. Co-Packaged Optics addresses these issues by enabling shorter distances for signal conversion, thereby improving performance and efficiency.
ai.manufacturing: The manufacturing process involves integrating photonic components onto the same substrate as the electronic components using advanced packaging techniques such as wafer-level bonding and assembly. This requires precise alignment and integration of materials at the nanoscale level to ensure reliable operation.
ai.buildProcess: A multi-step process involving wafer fabrication, die attachment, optical alignment, and encapsulation is used to assemble co-packaged optics. The alignment must be accurate to maintain signal integrity over short distances.
ai.costDrivers: High initial development costs due to the complexity of integrating photonic components with silicon electronics, precision manufacturing requirements, and specialized equipment for assembly. Long-term cost reductions are expected as production scales up.
ai.lifecycleOutlook: The technology is transitioning from early prototypes to commercialization stages but faces challenges in widespread adoption due to integration complexity and high initial costs.
ai.regulation: Current regulatory frameworks do not specifically address co-packaged optics, so compliance with general electronics manufacturing standards applies. However, safety regulations for optical components must be adhered to during design and production.
ai.risks: Technical risks include achieving reliable long-term performance of integrated photonic components, maintaining signal integrity over short distances, and ensuring compatibility across different silicon-based devices. Market risks involve the high initial investment required for adoption by manufacturers and data centers.
ai.profitability: Profitability is uncertain at this stage due to high development costs and limited market penetration. Potential profitability increases as production scales and more companies adopt the technology.
ai.futureDevelopment: Future developments may focus on improving integration techniques, reducing manufacturing costs, expanding application areas beyond AI clusters and data centers, and enhancing performance metrics such as bandwidth and power efficiency.

glossary.def: A technology that integrates optical interconnects directly onto the same package as electronic components to improve data transmission speed and efficiency.
Integrated photonic devices fabricated on a silicon wafer, used for converting electrical signals into light and vice versa in co-packaged optics systems.
Custom-designed integrated circuits optimized to perform specific tasks, commonly used in data centers and AI applications.

subsystems.name: Photonic integrated circuit (PIC)
subsystems.role: converts electrical signals to light and back on a silicon chip.

subsystems.name: Electronics IC (EIC)
subsystems.role: drives the modulators and amplifies the tiny photocurrents.

subsystems.name: Laser source
subsystems.role: supplies continuous light, kept off the hot package.

subsystems.name: Package substrate and interposer
subsystems.role: routes high-speed electrical and photonic signals between chips with fine pitch.

subsystems.name: Fibre attach and connector
subsystems.role: gets hundreds of optical channels in and out of the package reliably.

subsystems.name: Thermal and assembly housing
subsystems.role: keeps the optics cool next to a chip dissipating over a kilowatt.

buildSteps.title: Design the photonic and electronic dies together
buildSteps.detail: Waveguides, modulators and detectors are laid out in software that also co-simulates the driver and amplifier circuits, since the two must match electrically and optically.

buildSteps.title: Fabricate the PIC
buildSteps.detail: Silicon-on-insulator wafers run through a CMOS-compatible foundry: lithography and etching form waveguides, germanium is grown for detectors, and oxide cladding is deposited.

buildSteps.title: Fabricate the EIC
buildSteps.detail: Driver and amplifier circuits are made in a fast bipolar-CMOS process, then both wafers are tested at wafer level so only known-good dies go forward.

buildSteps.title: Bond dies to the package
buildSteps.detail: PIC and EIC are flip-chip bonded onto the interposer with micro-bumps, underfilled, and often stacked so the electronics sit directly on the photonics.

buildSteps.title: Attach the fibres
buildSteps.detail: A fibre array unit is aligned to the chip couplers — usually passively against etched alignment features, then actively fine-tuned — and fixed with adhesive cured under UV.

buildSteps.title: Connect the external lasers
buildSteps.detail: Laser modules are mounted away from the hot switch die and their light is routed in by fibre, so heat does not shorten laser life.

buildSteps.title: Assemble around the switch or processor
buildSteps.detail: The optical chiplets are placed in a ring on the same substrate as the main ASIC, then a lid and cold plate are fitted.

buildSteps.title: Test at full link speed
buildSteps.detail: Every optical lane is exercised end to end, then the package is temperature-cycled and burn-in tested before shipping.

prerequisites.why: plug-in optical transceivers already use silicon photonic chips in volume, proving the process.
bumping, interposers and fine-pitch substrates are needed to place optics beside logic.
a broken fibre in a sealed package would scrap an expensive board, so serviceable connectors with hundreds of channels are essential.

prerequisites.tech: Thermal control of a combined optical and logic package
prerequisites.why: lasers and modulators drift with temperature while the ASIC runs far hotter, and both share one package.
customers need optics from different suppliers to work with switches from different makers.

pathway.milestone: pluggable 800G and 1.6T optical transceivers dominate datacentre links
pathway.unlocks: a proven silicon photonics supply chain and a clear power-per-bit problem to solve.

pathway.milestone: co-packaged optics in first production switches for AI clusters
pathway.unlocks: lower power per bit and higher port counts at the front panel.

pathway.milestone: standardised optical chiplets with field-replaceable fibres
pathway.unlocks: optical I/O offered as a component, not a bespoke design.

pathway.milestone: optical links between accelerators and inside multi-chip packages
pathway.unlocks: disaggregated computing, where memory and compute sit metres apart.
